item.title: Fall Transitions: What Will You Harvest? What Let Go?
item.description:
Self-Help

Fall Transitions: What Will You Harvest? What Let Go?

As we enter autumn, what are you shedding so that something new can grow?

Posted August 29, 2026

Fall (2026) by Burt Kushner
Source: Burt Kushner / Used with permission

Wherever you live on this planet, you’ve experienced seasons. Seasons happen because Earth spins on a tilted axis. When the North Pole tilts toward the sun, it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere; when the South Pole tilts toward the sun, it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. In autumn, Earth is neither tilted toward nor away from the sun.1

Autumn, or fall, as we Americans call it, shortened from the 16th-century British expression “fall of the leaf,” is a transitional season bridging summer and winter, a time of harvest, of cooler, shorter days and thinning sunlight.

For many of us, it’s a time of endings—beach time, vacation time are over. Gone are the fireflies, butterflies, and pesky mosquitoes. The marigolds and petunias we planted in June are now shriveled brown blossoms. Our summer romances are over; the birds that sang to us through June, July, and August have departed. Canopies of green leaves that sheltered us from summer’s blaze are crispy around the edges. Like all living things, we feel the coming descent of the cold, dark months.

What does the arrival of this transitional season mean to you? What has been born in your inner world during the summer? What cycle has been completed? What are you looking forward to in the months to come?

The mythologist Michael Meade refers to autumn as a threshold time when old structures fall away.2 The shedding of old forms (or leaves!) is necessary for new growth. This is as true for us as it is for the trees in our forests: something must die for something new to be born. Our ancestors noted seasons by attending to the visible signs of change: the melting of lake ice, the ripening of berries, the disappearance of loons. What changes have occurred in your life recently? What new projects, ideas, inspirations, commitments have entered your world? What old story or pattern of behavior is asking to be shed? What emotional wound is ready to be harvested for the wisdom it has provided?

Psychiatrist, Jungian analyst, and author Jean Shinoda Bolen talks about transitional times as liminal spaces when we are at a threshold but have not moved through to the other side. This is like being in a waiting room, or as Bolen writes, like being inside a cocoon.3 Autumn into winter is a cocooning time, when we, like caterpillars, are preparing to transform. The long cold days of winter invite us to enjoy heavier meals, go to sleep earlier, move slower through our days. We leave behind the lightness and freedoms of summer and enter into a different landscape.

Your transition may involve a return to school or a new job or returning to an old job with a new attitude. We mark our transition with new clothes, a new haircut, starting a new diet, or joining a gym. But unlike the predictable cycles in nature, or the caterpillar that emerges from its cocoon as a butterfly, we don’t know how we will evolve. We can count on summer becoming autumn and winter following fall—but what does the metaphor of death and rebirth mean for you?

Every season sparks changes in our minds and bodies. In the fall, we respond to the shorter, cooler, darker days by producing more melatonin, which makes us sleepier during the day. Our appetite increases, and our mood, influenced by sunlight and lower dopamine and serotonin, may take a dive. The colder air dries out our skin and the fragile tissue inside our nostrils, making us more susceptible to nasal infections. We may even shed more hair during this season.4

We can think of autumn as the ancient Celts did, as a time when the veil between the visible and invisible worlds grew thin.5 What in summer was shrouded by leaf and flower now bares itself? What has become more visible to you in your inner or outer worlds? During this harvest season, what have you planted in your personal, work, or spiritual life that has borne fruit? What bounty will sustain you in the months ahead? What seeds lie dormant in your imagination?

What is the one word you would use to describe yourself now?

item.title: What We Must Lose and Mourn in a Successful Analysis
item.description:
Psychoanalysis

What We Must Lose and Mourn in a Successful Analysis

In psychoanalysis, we must lose to gain and grieve to move forward.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Successful psychoanalysis involves letting go of defenses and fantasies.
  • Analysis means grieving fantasies of perfect parents, partners, and unambivalent love.
  • These losses can be painful, and must be mourned.
"Abandoned," Fritz von Uhde
Source: National Museum in Warsaw/Public Domain

Change is hard and painful, and we usually fight against it, even as we claim to want it. This is especially true in psychoanalysis, where many of our earliest, most ingrained, and most precious fantasies and wishes are frequently dismantled and reassembled to allow us to function better as agentic adults in an indifferent world. Each loss is the subject of months if not years of work, though the losses often happen simultaneously. The hardest part of letting go of these fantasies, blind-spots, beliefs, and wishes is fully grieving what it will be like to move through the world without them. In their place are new beliefs, fantasies, and wishes that hopefully more closely approximate reality and allow the analysand to act more freely and with less unconscious drive towards repetition.

  1. The fantasy of perfect parents (especially the perfect opposite-sex parent) who love us unambivalently and remain omnipotent
  2. The fantasy of a perfect childhood, in which we are loved, protected, and untouched by trauma or difficulty
  3. The belief that a romantic partner can replace or recreate the wished-for perfect parent, caring for us as a child would be cared for
  4. The wish that the analyst will love us as a child, protect us, and recreate the wished-for parent
  5. The ability to avoid the discomfort of ambivalence and to split the world and people into neat categories of good and bad
  6. The fantasy of power and control, and the belief that we can control others enough to force them to meet our infantile need for unambivalent love and care
  7. The fantasy of exceptionalism, either exceptionally gifted and deserving of special treatment, or exceptionally damaged and deserving of special treatment
  8. The belief that we do not have an unconscious, that we are logical, rational, fully conscious beings, and in control of our thoughts, feelings, and actions
  9. The unawareness of how unconscious fantasy drives the repetition of relational patterns, and that conscious fears mask unconscious wishes
  10. The belief in a certain, unambiguous narrative about ourselves and our lives
  11. The wish that the past can be shed like a snakeskin—that simply avoiding reflection is enough to jettison its impact
  12. The belief that psychological symptoms reflect a discrete, treatable “brain disease,” rather than a murky mix of genetics, epigenetics, childhood experience, intergenerational trauma, and present difficulty
  13. The wish that treatment and cure can occur passively, “done to” us, without our having to communicate in words and do the difficult work of analysis
  14. The fantasy of the “magic pill,” a medication that will cure us of unhappiness, anxiety, existential angst, and neurosis
  15. The wish to hold onto old and familiar defense mechanisms that no longer provide comfort or safety, and no longer serve their old communicative purpose (denial, projection, intellectualization, externalization)
  16. The wish to hold onto old and familiar behaviors that no longer meet the need for protection or communication as they once did (binge eating, restrictive eating, self-harm, suicidal threats, splitting, indifference)
  17. The identity of “victim,” “patient,” or “damaged,” and the growing awareness, in its place, of one’s own autonomy and responsibility toward growth

The last point, about a developing awareness of our responsibility towards our own growth, may sound hopeful, like a gain and not a loss. I assure you it is one of the most painful losses—to truly let go of the wish for rescue by another, and understand that we are the only agents of change in our lives.

item.title: Why Forbidden Love Feels So Good
item.description:
Relationships

Why Forbidden Love Feels So Good

When breaking romantic rules doesn't mean breaking love.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Forbidden love derives much of its appeal from incompleteness, fantasy, novelty, risk, and meaning.
  • Unfinished romantic experiences often remain especially powerful because they are never fully resolved.
  • Minor romantic infringements are not always equivalent to fundamental betrayal.
  • Healthy relationships require both clear boundaries and reasonable flexibility.

We usually feel guilty after doing something forbidden. Forbidden love often has the opposite effect. It can feel exhilarating, meaningful, and intensely alive. Why are people so attracted to romantic boundaries they know they should not cross?

The Allure of Forbidden Love

"Stolen waters are sweet." —Proverbs 9:17

"There is a charm about the forbidden that makes it unspeakably desirable." —Mark Twain

Forbidden love involves romantic or sexual feelings, fantasies, or relationships that violate important social or personal norms. Yet not every forbidden act causes direct harm. Sometimes what makes something forbidden is simply that it crosses an accepted boundary. The digital age has made romantic transgressions easier. Online relationships blur traditional boundaries, partly because anonymity and distance reduce some of the social and emotional costs. People can now explore forbidden attractions from the privacy of their homes. Understanding the appeal of forbidden love does not mean endorsing it. The psychological forces that make forbidden relationships attractive can be genuine even when acting on them is harmful.

Why the Forbidden Is So Attractive

Source: Mario W/Pexels

Forbidden love draws its power from several sources: incompleteness, fantasy, meaning, novelty, and limited commitment.

1. Incomplete Experiences

"At my wedding, I wanted to have sex with my ex." —A woman

Incomplete romantic experiences often become emotionally powerful because they remain unresolved. Love may be present but never fully realized, creating a psychological tension that continues to demand attention. Unfinished experiences frequently remain more vivid than completed ones (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019). A forbidden relationship may therefore derive much of its appeal from what might have been rather than from what actually occurred. Unlike fulfilled relationships, it is spared the mundane realities that often accompany daily life together.

2. The Power of Fantasy

"My fantasy is to have five lovers. However, I do not think that my husband will agree, and anyway, I will not have time for having them all. I believe that three is the limit." —A married woman in a polyamorous relationship

Fantasy expands the romantic world beyond what we currently possess. Even people in loving relationships imagine alternative partners and alternative lives. The problem is that imagined possibilities are often compared with everyday reality. Real partners come with flaws, obligations, and conflicts. Imagined lovers rarely do. Fantasy can enrich romantic life, but it can also make reality seem unnecessarily mundane by idealizing possibilities that exist mainly in the imagination.

3. The Sense of Profound Meaning

"Anything without him couldn't be life at all. Since, and only since, I met him, I know why I have come to this world." —A woman describing her married lover

Forbidden love often acquires extraordinary significance precisely because it is difficult. The risks, sacrifices, and emotional investment involved can convince people that the relationship is uniquely valuable. Obstacles may create the feeling that the lovers share a private world, intensifying the belief that the relationship is most meaningful. The effort required to sustain the relationship becomes evidence, in the lovers' minds, of its importance. Research indeed suggests that people tend to value potential partners more highly when winning them requires effort, partly because investment increases perceived worth (Birnbaum et al., 2020).

4. Novelty Without Full Commitment

Forbidden love often combines two highly desirable qualities: novelty and limited commitment. Novelty fuels excitement and curiosity, while limited commitment spares people some of the burdens involved in building a shared life. An affair, for example, may provide the thrill of a new relationship without many of the practical challenges of long-term partnership. Yet healthy romantic life requires balancing novelty and commitment. Commitment should not suffocate spontaneity, but spontaneity should not undermine commitment.

How Should We Cope With Forbidden Love?

Responses to forbidden love generally take two forms. A prevention-oriented approach seeks to avoid temptation through boundaries and restrictions. A promotion-oriented approach focuses on strengthening intimacy, affection, and commitment. Because people are often more motivated by positive goals than by prohibitions, nurturing a fulfilling relationship may sometimes be more effective than multiplying restrictions.

1. Building Fences

"If it were not for evil desire, would man build a house, marry a wife, or have children?" —Genesis Rabbah 9:9

The desire for "more" is deeply human. One response is to build protective fences around existing boundaries. Many religious and social traditions have adopted such safeguards to reduce temptation and prevent serious violations. These measures can be effective. However, they may also prohibit behaviors that do not themselves violate the values the safeguards are designed to protect.

2. When Minor Infringements Occur

"If you are afraid of loneliness, do not marry." —Anton Chekhov

Human imperfection cannot be eliminated through rules alone. Some moral traditions recognize that the goal is not merely to prohibit wrongdoing but also to prevent occasional lapses from destroying broader values. This insight is psychologically important. Excessively rigid standards can sometimes encourage people to abandon those standards altogether once they inevitably fall short of them.

3. Bending Rather Than Breaking

"Better bend than break." —Scottish proverb

A crucial distinction exists between breaking a boundary and bending it. People may experience temptation without acting on it, fantasize without betraying, flirt without pursuing an affair, or make mistakes without becoming fundamentally unfaithful. Contrary to the popular saying, "Once a cheater, always a cheater," people are capable of learning, self-regulation, and change. The key question is not merely whether a boundary has been crossed, but what that crossing means for the relationship as a whole.

Romantic ideals become counterproductive when treated as inflexible, zero-tolerance standards. Sometimes flexibility protects an ideal better than rigidity. Bending does not necessarily mean abandoning values. It may mean adapting them to the complexities of real life. Of course, not all romantic infringements are minor. Adultery, deception, coercion, betrayal, and repeated violations of boundaries can inflict profound harm. Flexibility should never become an excuse for selfishness. Nevertheless, a minor deviation from a romantic ideal need not destroy the ideal itself. Sometimes absolute prohibition can be more damaging than acknowledging and responsibly managing human imperfection.

Concluding Thoughts

Forbidden love is attractive because it combines uncertainty, fantasy, novelty, risk, and meaning. What is difficult to obtain becomes especially desirable. People often tend to desire things more when our freedom to have them is restricted (Sinclair et al., 2015). Yet the fascination with forbidden love reveals a broader truth about relationships. Love requires boundaries, but it also requires flexibility. If every minor deviation is treated as a catastrophic betrayal, relationships may become more brittle rather than more secure. The challenge is not to eliminate temptation altogether. It is to preserve what matters most while recognizing that imperfect human beings, not idealized ones, are the people who love each other.

item.title: Can You Become More Extroverted? Would You Want To?
item.description:
Extroversion

Can You Become More Extroverted? Would You Want To?

The science of becoming more extroverted without becoming “an extrovert.”

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Both introversion and extraversion come with strengths.
  • Personality change means adjusting a trait, not jumping from one category to another.
  • Becoming more extroverted is useful when it helps you pursue something you value.
Source: Priscilla du Preez/Unsplash/Used with permission

Imagine you’re double-booked for a Friday night. One invitation is for a big party where you'll know only a handful of people. The other is for dinner with two close friends you've known for years. Which sounds better?

Your answer probably tells us something about your level of extraversion. People higher in extraversion tend to seek out social interaction and excitement. They're more likely to be talkative, assertive, energetic, and comfortable approaching people they don't know. They might also be prone to boredom and seek out new and stimulating activities.

People lower in extraversion tend to prefer less stimulation and may be more selective about their social interactions. Given the choice between a crowded party and dinner with a couple of close friends, they’d happily choose the latter.

Neither is inherently better. But what if being a little more extroverted would make it easier to create the life you want?

Why Would You Want to Become More Extroverted?

Extraversion is associated with some pretty appealing outcomes. People higher in this trait tend to experience more positive emotions and report greater well-being. Being comfortable approaching others can also make it easier to form relationships, build professional networks, and move up the ladder at work.

Given these benefits, it is natural to wonder if life would be easier if you were a bit more extroverted. Longitudinal research that follows people for decades tells us that traits evolve gradually across the lifespan, and more recently, researchers have studied whether it is possible to intentionally shift traits. The results of these studies suggest that when people are instructed to behave in more extroverted ways, like sharing more in social situations, they tend to get the benefits of being naturally higher in this trait, such as more positive emotions. Over time, these changes to behavior stick, and the dial on your extraversion goes up a bit.

But this doesn't mean everyone should be trying to become the life of the party. Personality change is only useful when it helps bring you closer to what you value.

There Are Benefits to Being More Introverted, Too

Just because there are benefits to being higher in extraversion doesn’t mean more of this trait is always better. People lower in extraversion may be more comfortable with solitude, less dependent on external stimulation, and more inclined to listen before jumping into a conversation. They may prefer a few close relationships to a large social network and be perfectly happy spending time on activities that don't involve other people.

These tendencies are real strengths. Someone who doesn't feel compelled to fill every silence may be a thoughtful listener. Someone who enjoys working independently may be able to spend long stretches focused on a project without needing much outside stimulation. And being selective about social activities can leave more time and energy for the relationships and other pursuits that most align with their values.

The goal of personality change isn't to move everyone toward the same supposedly ideal level of each personality trait. It's to figure out whether your current patterns are helping you create the life you want.

Think of a Dial, Not a Category

We often talk about introverts and extroverts as though they're two different kinds of people. But extraversion is a continuum. You can be relatively low, high, or, like most people, somewhere in between.

So becoming more extroverted doesn't require crossing some imaginary line from "introvert" to "extrovert." Think of it as turning a dial so that you can keep the benefits of introversion that serve you, while also unlocking new opportunities that being a bit more extroverted can offer. This could look like contributing a little more often in meetings when you usually stay quiet. You might consider agreeing to social activities you’d normally decline, especially if you genuinely want to build a new friendship.

Start With the Life You Want

How far you turn that dial, if at all, depends on what you want your life to look like. If you're happy with your relationships, enjoy how you spend your time, and don't feel that lower extraversion is getting in the way of anything important, there's no particular reason to change it. You do you.

Now imagine you want to move into leadership at work, but you rarely contribute during meetings. Or you've moved to a new city and need to make new friends. Perhaps you'd like a romantic relationship but rarely put yourself in situations where you might meet someone.

In those cases, becoming an extrovert still isn't the goal. The promotion, friendship, or relationship is the goal. Turning the dial slightly toward extraversion may simply help you get there.

item.title: Do You Still Long for the Ex You Never Had?
item.description:
Relationships

Do You Still Long for the Ex You Never Had?

How wishing for a missed romantic opportunity can stick with you.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • People who think back on an ex-partner with longing may be doing more than just being nostalgic.
  • A study of nostalgia for both current and ex-partners shows some of the dangers of dreaming about the past.
  • Think about past relationships not as they could have been but as they were, and your current one may improve.

It makes sense that you could, over time, develop a nostalgic fondness for an ex-partner. After all, with the passage of the months, years, or decades, what seemed like fatal flaws at the time evolve into minor obstacles that could easily have been overcome if only you stuck it out a little longer.

Beverly broke up with the partner she felt destined to marry when the arguments became more frequent and the kiss-and-make-up moments more rare. Now, 20 years later, she's happily married and generally satisfied with the way things turned out. But still her mind drifts to the what-ifs. She honestly can’t remember what all the fuss was about. All she can think about are the romantic evenings they spent having leisurely dinners by candlelight or just sitting on the couch in quiet conversation.

Time has a way of distorting the accuracy of memory for long-ago events, even for the most memorable of moments. What’s more, the factual accuracy may not jibe at all with the emotional flavor of those past events. Nostalgia has a way of making what was negative more positive and what were positive events become almost perfect in their recollection. Why, Beverly wonders, didn’t this relationship go from steady and serious to tied with a knot?

The Nature of Nostalgia for Exes

According to University of Texas psychologist Soo Yeon Park and colleagues (2026), this question doesn’t have much empirical research to draw upon for an answer. There is almost no research on ex-nostalgia, although what exists suggests that people who are happy in their current relationship are less likely to engage in this rumination about past relationships.

As theoretical background, the U. Texas authors draw on “motivated identity construction theory,” which suggests that people in longer-term relationships integrate ex-partner identities into their sense of self and accompanying life stories. Beverly, by this reasoning, has done just that. That ex of hers was someone who became part of her relationship life story. From that partnership, Beverly went on to form a new and now lasting partnership which, she believes, is pretty happy. But the “what if?” questions continue.

Testing Ex-Partner Nostalgia’s Predictors

Park et al. tested their ideas on a sample of 172 Korean adults, chosen because Korea represents a strongly relational culture in which people are highly attuned to close others in their lives. All participants were currently in a committed relationship but had at one point been in at least a three-month relationship.

The authors manipulated nostalgia by inducing either ex-nostalgia, current-nostalgia, or neither. One ex-nostalgia group wrote about nostalgic events with their ex, and the second about nostalgic events with their current partner; the neither group wrote about what they did during the previous week. Measures of relationship satisfaction with the current partner served as the outcome variable, with factors such as length of relationship with the ex (and time since then) as controls.

Contrary to prediction, both types of nostalgia induction positively affected current relationship satisfaction. Taking time into account and looking at commitment to the current partner, commitment in shorter relationships decreased after the current relationship nostalgia induction. The authors concluded that by focusing on the past with their current partner, participants were prompted to see their future as less certain. Maybe romanticizing the better days isn’t such a good thing if it causes you to wonder how long the good times will last.

Commitment did a flip-flop for ex-partner nostalgia. People induced to remember the good times with their ex felt more commitment to their current partners. This suggests that rather than shoving those thoughts out of your mind about the fun you had with your ex, you might be better off letting them drift in (at least from time to time) in terms of feelings toward the person you're with now.

Longing vs. Nostalgia

The Park et al. study provides intriguing insights into the nature of ex-partner reflection. As the authors point out, the fact that it was carried out in Korea suggests that reminiscing about a past relationship reflects their collectivist culture. Individualists may reflect on how a relationship affected their personal growth now, but collectivists may emphasize where the events occurred, and who else was there at the time.

Returning to the question of longing for that ex-partner, the identity framework suggests that when thinking about the past that never was, you don’t have any “data” to input into your sense of self with respect to that past partner. Everything stopped when that relationship ended. Therefore, all that’s left to do is engage in idle speculation. With your current partner, for better or worse, you know what did happen, and some of this could spell trouble for your thoughts about the future. You’ll never know what might have happened with the ex.

That open space allows all kinds of hyperbolically positive memories to enter. There you were at that candlelit dinner, staring into each other’s eyes and thinking loving thoughts. You have nothing to prompt, as you do with your current partner, what might be recent memories of disagreements or misunderstandings. The past can be perfect because it doesn’t have the present to interfere with that rosy glow.

It’s important to note that a constant immersion in the ex you never committed to could create problems if it dulls the pleasure you derive from your current partner. Nostalgia is one thing; longing is quite something else. If it’s continued desire that is driving your recollection, it may be time to look at what's missing in your current relationship. Maybe you can bring some of the spark from the relationship that never happened into the relationship that exists now.

To sum up, relationships become an integral part of our identity, even those relationships that didn’t materialize into something concrete. You’ll never know what might have happened, but you are living out the life that did.

item.title: How 'Cushioning' Can Be a Problem in Dating
item.description:
Mating

How 'Cushioning' Can Be a Problem in Dating

This dating trend can be a big red flag when you are supposed to be exclusive.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • "Cushioning" is maintaining backup people to date in case the current relationship does not work out.
  • Cushioning is essentially micro-cheating or even actual cheating, such as staying in close contact with exes.
  • People cushion out of insecurity, the fear of being single, or the desire to date other people.
  • When you suspect cushioning, be frank and open with your partner about your concerns and check the response.
"Cushioning" is maintaining backups when dating someone—backup people to date in case the current relationship does not work out for whatever reason.
Source: Andrea Piacquadio/Pexels

If the person you are dating offers you seat cushions whenever you sit down, your reaction might be "sofa" so good. However, it can be a very different story if he or she is "cushioning" himself or herself. That's because "cushioning" on social media and the Internet has come to mean the practice of maintaining backups when dating someone—backup people to date in case the current relationship does not work out for whatever reason.

What Is 'Cushioning'?

The term “cushioning" comes from the phrase "cushion your fall." Now, it may be natural to continue to date multiple people before you've gone exclusive with someone. However, once you're my-one-and-only with each other, the expectation usually is that neither of you will continue to keep others around as dating possibilities. Not everyone follows that dating convention, though.

Your significant other, for example, may continue to flirt with other people. This includes any behavior signaling to others that he or she is still available as a dating option. In fact, your significant other may not even tell others that you are his or her significant other. A possible sign of cushioning is when your significant other is significantly secretive about others.

You can put a big "ex" on a common source of cushioning as well. That's because when your partner stays in close contact with an ex or exes, he or she could be maintaining a rather familiar and thus comfortable cushion or exit ramp. The same applies to that close "platonic" friend whom your partner insists that he or she would never date but somehow always seems to turn to when the two of you have an argument.

Then there's the situation where your partner hasn't taken down his or her Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, or Mullet Passions dating profile yet. It's even more egregious when your significant other stays active in some way on such apps. Basically any type of microcheating, which I've covered before in "A Funny Bone to Pick," can be cushioning. So can any type of outright cheating.

Why Do People Practice Cushioning?

Such cushioning isn't just pillow talk. It's a sign that at least one of four things is happening. One is your partner being insecure and believing that your current relationship will not last. This worry can be particularly prominent if your partner can't stand being single

Insecure people may also crave the validation that they may get from others pursuing them. This is the "I've still got it" reassurance, where "it" is the ability to replace you very quickly. Validation is one reason why some people stay on dating apps.

A second possibility is your partner trying to maintain leverage and hold unrealistic expectations. Cushioning can give your partner an out as soon as you don't provide exactly what he or she wants. Dating app use may be contributing to the illusion that a replacement partner, like toilet paper, is just a swipe away.

A third possibility is your partner preparing for a breakup without telling you. Because why should you know? Indeed, cushioning could be your partner getting his or her duck pillows in a row so that he or she can readily transition into another relationship while you are left with the fall.

Finally, your partner could be very indecisive or even not able to commit to one person. Just because you've been declared "mi amor" doesn't always mean that your partner doesn't actually want "more amor." Your partner could be "monkey barring," too. This is where someone keeps trying to swing up progressively to more prized partners, as I've covered in "A Funny Bone to Pick."

What to Do When You Suspect Cushioning

Assuming that you aren't a fan of any of the above possibilities, what, then, should you do if you suspect your partner of being a cushioner? Well, if it's just a gut feeling without any real evidence, double-check first that it's not just your insecurity talking. Know yourself well—like what you may be projecting onto your partner. At the same time, don't be too quick to dismiss your gut feelings.

Consider having a real "pillow" talk, being open and frank with your partner about any concerns that you may have. After all, good free-flowing communication is the hallmark of a good relationship. That doesn't necessarily mean picking a "pillow" fight every time your partner says something friendly to an attractive server at a restaurant. But it helps for your partner to know you and your thoughts better.

Choose a time instead when the two of you can have an earnest, honest, and non-accusatory conversation privately. Then see how your partner reacts. You can emphasize that you don't want to jump to conclusions but are worried that your partner is not as all-in or committed to the relationship as you are.

If your partner isn't cushioning in any way, then the landing should be fairly soft. He or she should be able to confidently reassure you and may even be happy that you are so committed. If, on the other hand, your partner gets super defensive or reacts disproportionately harshly, this could be a red flag in and of itself.

When there's clearer evidence that cushioning is occurring, don't table it. Call it out as soon as possible but not in a combative way. Calmly indicate that you noticed, for example, that your partner is still on dating apps, regularly conversing with an ex, introducing you to others as just a friend, or telling others, "Are you a campfire? Because you're hot and I want s'more." See how direct, clear, and plausible your partner's responses and proposed rectifying actions are.

If you aren't fully satisfied with the responses, it may be time to end the relationship. Without mutual trust, it's hard to maintain any type of healthy relationship. And any type of cushioning greatly dampens such trust. You can't really couch it in any other way.

item.title: BPC-157: Miracle Drug or Joe Rogan Experiment?
item.description:
Health

BPC-157: Miracle Drug or Joe Rogan Experiment?

Why some people are so excited about experimental drugs with no human safety data.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • There have been only three small human trials of BPC-157.
  • Despite the lack of safety data, online interest has surged.
  • This appears to be due to a mixture of shrewd marketing and influencer endorsements.

If you’re among the majority of people who get their health and fitness advice online, you’d be forgiven for thinking that experimental peptides were like vegetables or exercise: the more the better, and in any variety. But beneath the hype and influencer rhetoric lies a wellness campaign that increasingly attempts to subvert the evidence safety net. In fact, on the risk-to-benefit scale, there’s remarkably little tipping toward benefit.

At the forefront of this movement is BPC-157, named after its primary function, “body protection compound,” followed by a numerical identifier that may as well be a factory label. The peptide was originally derived from a protein found in human gastric juice and was later synthesized as a 15-amino-acid peptide. Those who study the drug, as well as influencers grabbing at the veneer of scientific credibility, refer to it as a pentadecapeptide, a technical-sounding name for a peptide made of 15 amino acids ("penta-" meaning five and "deca-" meaning ten). Like many peptides, BPC-157 acts as a signaling molecule; like a line of code in a computer program, it dishes out instructions for which tasks to execute.

Widely used for “faster recovery,” particularly for healing tendons and soft tissue, BPC-157 has earned a fanbase among athletes, bodybuilders, fitness enthusiasts, and people with chronic pain. It’s also gained traction for its vaguely defined “gut healing” properties, making it popular among people dealing with ulcers and inflammatory bowel issues. After generating buzz within the biohacking community, BPC-157 really took off thanks to coverage from high-profile podcasters like Joe Rogan. He has mentioned the peptide in no fewer than 31 episodes, including one with Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who vowed to lift FDA restrictions on the peptide. Its powerful reputation for rejuvenation earned it the nickname the "Wolverine peptide," after the mutant Marvel antihero with regenerative abilities.

What the Science Says About BPC-157

Interest in BPC-157 actually dates back several decades to a single research group that would come to dominate the field. The research ambled for years in the preclinical space, with more than 150 studies eventually comprising the broader BPC-157 literature, exploring effects ranging from wound and tendon healing to inflammation and organ injury.

While some findings are striking, at least on paper, its name, “body protection compound,” is misleading; the bodies it supposedly protects aren’t even human. Indeed, nearly all the experimental literature consists of preclinical studies, primarily in rodents. These studies typically involve experimentally injuring a tendon or other tissue in rats before administering BPC-157, sometimes alongside corticosteroids or saline as a control. BPC-157-treated rats often heal faster, maintain better tissue integrity, and regain normal function more quickly than controls. Other experiments report effects across a broad range of tissues and organ systems, including angiogenesis (blood vessel proliferation), nitric oxide signaling, inflammation, and tissue repair. It’s an unusual breadth of potential applications.

The problem, of course, is that rodents aren’t people. True, they have a circulatory system and many of the same organs, but they differ in metabolism, immune function, and disease biology. Work on the peptide never transitioned from preclinical literature into robust human trials; essentially, BPC-157 never graduated from preschool. More conspicuously, more than 80% of the published evidence comes from one interconnected Croatian research program centered at the University of Zagreb, with comparatively little independent replication.

That’s hardly the résumé of a game-changing drug.

Human Trials of BPC-157

Only three published human studies are available to discuss. One, published in 2021, examined the peptide’s effect on knee pain; another, published in 2024, looked at interstitial cystitis, also known as Bladder Pain Syndrome; and a third, published in 2025, was a two-person pilot study assessing the tolerance of intravenous BPC-157 administered over just three days. These studies comprise just 30 people, and none was randomized or placebo-controlled. The knee study was a retrospective chart review rather than a prospective trial. As a clinically meaningful body of work, these data are next to useless. In scientific circles, BPC-157 is the firework that never ignited.

Online, however, its popularity has exploded. Online ads for these “problematic peptides” increased nearly eightfold since 2022, while Google search interest reached a peak in 2024 and has only increased, largely due to coverage from Rogan and others. There are around 165,000 “BPC-157” online searches every month, making it one of the largest non-weight-loss peptide search terms.

It’s a symptom of a broader problem. Today’s wellness economy commodifies natural, holistic interventions. Peptides are largely framed as “recovery” and “rejuvenation” protocols that feel distinct from the aesthetic interventions classically favored by bodybuilders and fitspiration influencers. And the idea of “healing” makes people less squeamish about using peptides, most of which require injection. Incredibly, their lack of human data is effectively framed as a positive, dovetailing neatly into an anti-science narrative that has cast health professionals as greedy corporate shills who want nothing more than to keep wellness purists dependent on regulated drugs.

Why Experimental Peptides Go Viral

Experimental peptides like BPC-157 let consumers believe they’re regaining control over their wellness and subverting medical orthodoxy. It’s part of an ongoing narrative, spurred on by the COVID-19 pandemic, about breaking free of medicine’s institutional shackles through our wellness choices; a narrative in which the absence of human safety data is somehow part of the sales pitch. Of course, it’s all rhetoric; experimental peptides are manufactured through the same modern pharmaceutical and biotechnology infrastructure that wellness purists supposedly distrust, just without the data safety net.

Peptides thrive online because they feed into a digital economy that rewards simple, confident advice. Nobody wants to believe that healing takes time, that fitness is hard-won, or that long-term weight loss requires a lifestyle overhaul. They’d rather take the pill, drink the powder, and inject the serum. Experimental peptides offer everything humans have coveted in wellness since wellness became a thing: a different compound for every ailment—skin, muscle, fat loss, recovery, longevity. It’s absolutism that is the antithesis of science.

We shouldn’t be surprised by the meteoric rise of experimental peptides like BPC-157. It's the inevitable product of an online culture where fitness influencers and podcasters with commercial conflicts of interest have become the principal arbiters of health, wellness, and performance advice. Online algorithms prize simple, sensational content because it will always outperform the mundane. It’s a problem that will only worsen as social media tightens its hold on health advice.

Combating Misinformation About Peptides

The answer isn’t simply to crack down on social media misinformation; that requires platform buy-in and federal regulation, neither of which is forthcoming. Rather, scientists and medical professionals need to do more to puncture the misinformation bubble and make their voices heard. We’ll never be as loud as the wellness influencers or pseudoscientists because our message isn’t as sexy, but by making the tools available and giving people access to the evidence rather than merely the sales pitch, we can at least give the public a fighting chance to make informed decisions about the benefits and risks of their wellness pursuits.

Every intervention involves a balance between risk and benefit. Science doesn’t eliminate that uncertainty; it merely quantifies it. With BPC-157 and its contemporaries, the risks don’t outweigh the benefits, because we don’t even have enough data to know how the scales will tip.

item.title: How to Have a Healthy Sex Life With Mental Illness
item.description:
Sex

How to Have a Healthy Sex Life With Mental Illness

What you can do to help build intimacy when you have a mental illness.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Mental illness symptoms can detract from connecting with a partner during intimacy.
  • Feeling safe in one's body is the key factor in building a healthy sex life with mental illness.
  • It is possible to work through symptoms such as PTSD, anxiety, and loss of self toward a healthy sex life.

Do you live with a mental illness that impacts your sex life? Have you ever wanted to feel closer to your partner even if your mind (or your body) is telling you to fear them? Do you experience things like your body shutting down and numbing during intimate moments?

Sex therapy and classic psychotherapy are typically segregated in clinical care, when in fact, they are integrated. But what would you find out if you could learn from both expertises?

Gaby Balsells is a clinical psychologist and relationship coach who works with individuals and couples all over the world. In this post, we discuss ways to establish a healthy sex life, so that someone living with a mental condition doesn’t have to sacrifice the things that make their life fulfilling.

How to Build a Healthy Sex Life With Your Mind, Body, and Partner

SAM: Living with mental illness can make a person feel unsafe, insecure, or even afraid to communicate with their partner about what they are thinking and feeling. Can you first explain what makes a healthy sex life? How should we approach sex when there are vulnerabilities?

GB: A “healthy” sex life is one in which you can feel both safe and fulfilled erotically. So what that looks like will be different for everyone, because we all have different needs, desires, and bodies.

At its core, a healthy sex life involves being embodied–or in touch with your own body–and being able to experience pleasure and aliveness within yourself as well as in connection with another person or people. It also involves a sense of agency through feeling like you can not only identify your desires and needs and communicate openly about them, but also having the ability to shift the direction of a sexual experience so that it becomes more aligned with what feels fulfilling for you.

Essentially, healthy sex is not about one specific recipe or frequency. It’s when we have the safety, freedom, and capacity to curate experiences by our own design, and that includes the ingredients that feel authentically pleasurable and meaningful to you and your partner(s).

SAM: Mental illness can take many forms, so I am wondering about specific symptoms that can affect one's sex life. In particular, how can you have a healthy sex life when you have PTSD from sexual trauma, an unstable sense of self, or even hallucinations, delusions, and paranoia about your partner?

GB: Mental illness symptoms like these impact one’s sex life because they involve a loss of safety via disconnection from your body, from the present moment, and/or disconnection from your partner or lover. When this happens, symptoms can cause two alternatives: numbing/dissociating or activation/fear (a.k.a. freaking out).

When that is the case, what is needed is a practice of returning to safety. Safety in your own body, in the moment, and in your relationship. This might look like taking breaks during sex, self-soothing, and adding in practices of “sensual mindfulness”—reconnecting to stimulus and to your senses as a way of coming back to your body and to presence. This is something a therapist or intimacy coach can support you with.

What’s important to understand is that these issues can act as a direct brake on arousal and pleasure. When symptoms pull you out of the sexual experience, it may not be realistic—or even helpful—to rush back to or try to jump back into sex. Instead, take a few steps back to re-establish safety first, reconnect with your body and your senses second, and then, from that place, begin to introduce sexual contact or experiences that can support arousal and pleasure.

This can feel frustrating because it may seem like you’re moving backward when what you really want is to move forward. But most times, taking those few steps back is exactly what allows you to spring forward. The goal isn’t to rush past the symptoms or disconnection, but to create enough safety so that when it happens, you can notice, catch it, and find your way back to either relaxation or even to pleasure/arousal becoming accessible again.

SAM: Why do you think sexual health has been neglected in treating mental illness? And do you often treat both at the same time?

GB: Even though sexuality is such an important part of a holistic view of a person’s life, sexual health is still significantly underdeveloped in many clinical training programs and professional education. As a result, many clinicians don’t have the specialized expertise to work with sexuality, particularly at the intersection of sexuality and mental health.

Additionally, both topics still hold a lot of taboos and shame, which can make them difficult to bring up and talk about openly for both clients and clinicians. When you combine that discomfort with limited training, sexuality can easily become an area that gets left out of the conversation or treatment plan, even though it’s such a key piece of holistic health.

I do often treat both at the same time, and my current work focuses on the intersection of mental illness and sexuality. I like to say my work is not only trauma-informed but also sex-positive and pleasure-informed. It means no shame or judgment, so that my client’s feelings, desires, and questions are all safe to bring into the room.

SAM: Do you have a successful story of a couple or individual becoming able to manage their symptoms and have a thriving sex life?

GB: Yes. I’ve worked with couples where PTSD symptoms were showing up during sexual intimacy and making it difficult for one or both partners to stay present and connected. In one case, one partner would experience intense shifts between fear, anger, and disconnection, going from hot to cold or even angry during the same sexual experience. This was confusing and painful for their partner, and the person experiencing those reactions carried significant guilt, which created a cycle of anxiety around initiation, response, and intimacy, as well as a ton of sexual shame and relational frustration.

Through our work together, I provided attachment healing and trauma processing, as well as sex education that helped the couple expand how they communicated about desire, arousal, boundaries, and safety. We also worked on self-soothing and recognizing early signs of activation so they could respond differently in the moment, as well as partnered intimacy exercises and rituals.

Over time, they developed much more confidence and compassion around these experiences, were able to interrupt the fear-and-guilt cycle, and ultimately create a sexual relationship that felt safer, more connected, and genuinely pleasurable for both partners.

item.title: The Metaphysics of Contact
item.description:
Cognition

The Metaphysics of Contact

What a tennis ball reveals about the limits of measurement.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • A stroke pulls together coiling, ground force, wind and spin. Contact is just a few milliseconds of it.
  • The strings only ever meet a compressed sphere. They don't feel the ball.
  • Expert athletes' brains prepare a response to the sounds of their own sport.
  • fMRI measures a blood flow response four to six seconds late, not neurons firing.
Contact as a short sliver of reality
Source: DALL·E through ChatGPT

When a person hits a tennis ball, the moment of contact is infinitesimally small: A few milliseconds when the ball lands on the strings, which stretch backward ever so slightly and then slingshot the ball forward and up into the court.

Thinking that science measures reality is like thinking that everything about a tennis shot can be determined by the measurement of contact.

But a tennis stroke consists of movement to the ball. The coiling and stretching of various muscles. Compressing one's legs and using the ground to propel the force through the feet and the legs, up through the torso, which uncoils as the force moves through into the shoulder, the arm, and finally the hands.

Contact occurs.

Then the ball travels through the air, interacting with gravity, wind, and the texture of the court that changes the spin the ball has.

If a tennis player were a scientist, she would only be able to measure the very moment of impact. It is the only point at which the instrument touches what is being studied. The only moment at which the strings meet a compressed sphere.

Timothy Morton, in Humankind, puts it plainly: science "can never directly talk about reality, only about data."

It turns out that the strings don't actually hit a ball. At least not the one I see inside the tennis can when I open it and pull it out. Not the one that comes out of my pocket. When the ball hits the strings it compresses, distorts itself, and becomes flatter, much less round than it is when we watch it by itself.

The strings don't know anything about all of this. The only thing they experience is a compressed sphere. They have no idea that the sphere lives in a can, that it was produced in a factory, that it wears down and goes dead as time passes.

The strings only experience something compressing against them, their own stretching backwards, and the propulsion forward.

A player has much more than just the strings' contact with the ball. When you hit a tennis ball, you feel the reverberation in the frame. You feel the breeze and its direction. You see the trajectory of the ball as it flies through the air, anticipating where the next ball will land and what you need to do about it.

Every one of those is a small window into what will happen. They are separate instances, things that could be measured. When I am playing, I am putting them all together in one motion, one package, combined.

It might be data. But it is the combination of them that is interesting.

Many years ago in our lab, in a study headed by Elizabeth Woods, now a professor at Texas Lutheran University, we asked athletes to listen to sounds from their own sport or from another sport. These were tennis players and basketball players, lying in a scanner, not asked to do anything at all.

What we found was that the sounds from their own sport activated motor planning and sensory areas of the right hemisphere. Areas that on the left would be involved in language, on the right are involved in preparation for action.

We compared college athletes with those who played less often. They had played about the same number of years, but what separated them was practice—14 hours a week versus five—and having started to play at a younger age. The college athletes activated these areas as if the sound prepared a motor response. The novices activated many more. Wide swaths of the brain, working to make sense of what they were hearing. The experts' responses were tuned to the sounds of their sport and their brains cleanly prepared a response, even when there was no response required.

So contact isn't just the contact for the person hitting the ball. It is also the sound of the other person's contact, heard before the ball is on its way.

Even that finding comes to us secondhand. fMRI relies on changes in deoxyhemoglobin. When an area becomes active, blood flow to it increases, and more oxygen arrives than the tissue actually uses. That signal is not the neurons firing. It is a vascular response that peaks four to six seconds later. Like the strings, the scanner touches a distorted version of the thing it is measuring.

For the longest time I practiced at full speed. But Tomaz Mencinger taught me something I didn't expect. His idea was that tennis could be played at a much slower speed. He calls his approach Feel Tennis. How does the ball feel to you? How do things feel when you move?

Under his guidance I began to play slower. Just feeling the contact of the ball, the moment when the ball hits the strings. I began to focus on watching and feeling, as well as I could, the contact of the ball on the strings. Focusing on that very small moment when we actually control what the ball is going to do.

When we make that moment longer (at least in my mind it feels longer), the stroke improves.

This may sound like a contradiction but it isn't one. A scientist can peel everything away, leaving the contact as an isolated data point. As a human and a player, I take that very moment and pull it toward all the other things that come before and after it. The wind. The sound. The frame. The same instant, the opposite operation.

Science may be able to cut these things apart, to separate them, to compartmentalize them. Brain scientists often look for very specific brain signatures for very specific cognitive signals. The movements we make. The sounds we hear. The sights we see. Even the feelings we feel.

But it is only in the combination of all of those into a whole that our reality presents itself. Only in the phenomenology, the word philosophers use for the way reality appears to us. It arrives as an experience. And that is the difference between science and being human.

Only there can we see and understand how it is possible that infinitely small windows can still make the ball land in.
